full_text: IJBPAS, September, 2026, 15(9): 4327-4337 ISSN: 2277–4998 4327 IJBPAS, September, 2026, 15(9) A COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW ARTICLE ON EXPANDING HPV VACCINATION HORIZONS IN INDIA: EVIDENCE FOR ONE-DOSE SCHEDULES AND MALE INCLUSION SRAVANTHI MALISETTY CLS1*, HARSHA VARDHINI K R1, SRUTHI D1, JAHNAVI K1, T. JAI DIVYA2 AND RAMA RAO N3 1: Chalapathi Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Affiliated by ANU, Chalapathi, Nagar, Lam, Andhra Pradesh 522034 2: Assistant Professor, Chalapathi Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Affiliated by ANU, Chalapathi, Nagar, Lam, Andhra Pradesh 522034 3: Principal, Professor, Chalapathi Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Affiliated by ANU, Chalapathi, Nagar, Lam, Andhra Pradesh 522034 *Corresponding Author: Chatana Lakshmi Sai Sravanthi Malisetty: E Mail: krhvardhini2005@gmail.com https://doi.org/10.31032/IJBPAS/2026/15.9.10462 ABSTRACT In India, cervical cancer continues to affect many women, though it is largely preventable through HPV vaccines. Recent Indian studies suggest that a single dose may be enough for lasting protection, which is especially useful where access to healthcare is limited. There is rising focus on vaccinating boys, which provides protection against HPV-associated cancers in males while also decreasing community-level infection. The evidence reviewed here points to the potential of these interventions to fast-track India’s efforts in meeting cervical cancer elimination targets. Keywords: Human papillomavirus; Single-dose HPV vaccination; Male HPV vaccination; Cervical cancer prevention; Gender-neutral immunization; Cost-effectiveness; India; Cervavac INTRODUCTION Given the global cervical cancer burden, India bears nearly 20%, with reports around 123,000 of new diagnosis and 77,000 deaths per year [1]. The types 16 and 18 are the Received 29th Sept. 2025; Revised 18th Oct. 2025; Accepted 22nd March 2026; Available online 1st Sept. 2026 Sravanthi Malisetty CLS et al Review Article 4328 IJBPAS, September, 2026, 15(9) high-risk HPV strains which show a persistent infection hold account for nearly 70% of these cases [1, 5]. Protection against HPV16/18 persists for at least 5 years after a single dose [17]. Despite the proven role of HPV vaccination, two- or three dose schedules remain the global standard. Evidence is increasingly showing that a one- dose regimen could achieve adequate and sustained defence against infection [1-3]. At the same time, shifted interest in vaccinating boys enhances its potential to boost herd immunity and reduce the wider impact of HPV associated cancers in both genders. So, while still making cervical cancer elimination as the primary goal, we need to make sure to follow gender neutral vaccination and simple one dose regimen which helps in redefining the strategy on india. One-dose HPV vaccination could prevent a majority of cervical cancers in India, making it highly cost-effective [11]. The review highlights the India’s shifting HPV vaccination policies, focusing on research that validates one-dose protection and the public health benefits of male vaccination. THE CRITICAL ROLE OF HPV VACCINATION IN CANCER PREVENTION: A single dose of HPV vaccine can help cut down cervical cancer incidence and reduce overall costs in India, though gaps in vaccination coverage remain a concern [36, 37]. In South Asia, uptake is low at about 8%, but improving knowledge and awareness can increase acceptance. Even with lower antibody responses, a single dose still provides effective protection compared with multiple doses [38, 39]. HPV vaccines are widely regarded as safe, protective, and economically beneficial. Offering a single dose to 10-year-old girls in India proves more cost-effective than giving two doses [40, 41]. The recently tested quadrivalent vaccine has shown excellent safety and immune response in both girls and boys aged 9–14, and both one- and two-dose regimens work well if given before exposure [42, 43]. India’s indigenous vaccine highlights progress, yet barriers like limited awareness and access continue. Long-term results reveal about 95% protection up to 10 years, supporting inclusion in the UIP [44, 45]. Widespread adolescent vaccination could prevent up to 90% of cervical cancer cases. Persistent hurdles include limited epidemiological clarity, mixed parental attitudes, and gaps in monitoring. Vaccine efficacy remains highest when given between ages 9 and 14 [46-48]. A single dose has shown strong protection against HPV-16 in Indian girls, yet overall uptake in South Asia is still poor, with awareness continuing to be the strongest predictor of acceptance [49, 50]. EVIDENCE FOR ONE DOSE HPV VACCINATON IN INDIA: Sravanthi Malisetty CLS et al Review Article 4329 IJBPAS, September, 2026, 15(9) Indian research, in collaboration with IARC, provides robust data validating the effectiveness of single-dose HPV vaccination. Basu et al. [1, 18] reported long-term outcomes showing that protection against HPV-16/18 infection persisted for at least a decade, with efficacy from a single dose approximating that of multidose regimens. Longitudinal immunogenicity analysis also confirmed durable antibody levels after one dose [2], and further observational work showed reduced new HPV infections [5]. Economic and modeling analyses further emphasize the potential of this approach, showing that single-dose programs could be both impactful in reducing cervical cancer and financially practical for India [3, 4, 16]. Studies indicate that a one-dose HPV vaccination plan offers nearly 50% savings compared to multi-dose regimens while still delivering strong protection levels. For resource-constrained settings such as India, this cost-effectiveness could make large-scale vaccination programs more feasible. Yet, it remains important to track recipients long-term to confirm durability and address potential risks of waning immunity. Single-dose schedules provide comparable long-term protection as two- or three-dose regimens [12, 15, 19, 20]. Single-dose vaccination effectively reduces cervical precancerous lesions (CIN2+) [30]. Table 1: Comparision between one dose and multi dose schedule [12, 26, 30, 31, 43] PARAMETER ONE DOSE SCHEDULE MULTI-DOSE SCHEDULE Efficacy against HPV 16/18 infecion Comparable protection sustained for 10 years or more High protection but requires 2-3 doses for full effect Antibody response Stable and durable after one dose Higher initial antibody levels but similar long term protection Cost effectiveness 40-50% cheaper and easier to implement More expensive due to multiple doses and logistics Feasibility in low resource settings Simplified logistics and better compliance Difficult due to repeated visits and higher cost Protection duration Proven protection up to 10 years Long term protection established but depends on full schedule Public acceptance Increasing awareness and acceptance Acceptable but compliance drops due to multiple visits Sravanthi Malisetty CLS et al Review Article 4330 IJBPAS, September, 2026, 15(9) Figure 1: Rationale for one-dose HPV vaccination in India [1, 3, 11] MALE HPV VACCINATION: RATIONALE AND EVIDENCE HPV vaccination is primarily targeted at cervical cancer prevention, yet males remain at risk for several HPV-associated malignancies, including anal, penile, and oropharyngeal cancers. A systematic review by Ferrandiz-Pulido et al. [6] reported substantial evidence that vaccination is highly effective in protecting males against persistent HPV infection. Trials of India’s home grown vaccine, Cervavac, demonstrated robust immune responses and a favourable safety profile among 9–14- year-old boys and girls, performing on par with Gardasil [7]. Vaccinating boys provides them direct protection and enhances herd immunity by lowering overall viral spread. Antibody responses in males after one dose support the inclusion of boys in vaccination programs [13]. Expanding HPV vaccination to males reframes the program as a universal health intervention rather than a women-only measure. Alongside reducing stigma, it provides crucial protection against male cancers like oropharyngeal, anal, and penile cancers, which are increasingly recognized as a growing burden in India. Gender-neutral HPV vaccination can reduce HPV transmission and protect both sexes effectively [14, 29]. Sravanthi Malisetty CLS et al Review Article 4331 IJBPAS, September, 2026, 15(9) Figure 2: Indian burden map [27, 37, 47] POSITIONING INDIA WITHIN THE GLOBAL HPV ELIMINATION EFFORT: The Kenyan KEN SHE study provided compelling evidence that a single HPV vaccine dose can offer substantial protection for adolescent girls, bolstering the argument for streamlined vaccine regimens in low- and middle-income regions [8]. In South Asia, however, progress has been uneven, with ongoing obstacles such as reluctance toward vaccination, gender-related inequalities, and gaps in health infrastructure [9]. Initial trials of Cervavac in Indian adults confirmed its favourable safety profile [10], which supports its integration into large-scale programs. With its cost-effective local production, strong one-dose data, and the potential for vaccinating boys, India has a chance to spearhead global initiatives aimed at eliminating cervical cancer. HPV vaccine uptake in India is hindered by cultural perceptions linking it to sexual activity, low awareness in rural communities, and limited school-based delivery. Digital health tools, engagement of ASHA workers, and targeted social media campaigns can help address misinformation and improve coverage [21, 22]. Cultural beliefs and misinformation can affect vaccine acceptance in rural India [24, 34]. Cervavac offers an affordable indigenous option and strengthens India’s role in global health [28, 33]. Sravanthi Malisetty CLS et al Review Article 4332 IJBPAS, September, 2026, 15(9) Figure 3: Diagram of immune response between one dose and multiple dose [2, 5, 16, 17] POLICY IMPLICATIONS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS: India’s commitment to the WHO target of cervical cancer elimination by 2030 underscores the urgency of adopting innovative vaccination strategies. A single- dose schedule could significantly improve uptake and adherence, especially among rural and marginalized groups [3, 4]. Integrating boys into routine programs could normalize HPV vaccination as a shared responsibility while reducing inequities [6, 7]. Future studies should emphasize long- term follow-up of one-dose recipients, evaluate Cervavac’s effectiveness in real- world settings, and design practical frameworks for including boys in the national program. Integrating HPV vaccination into the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) with school-based initiatives can promote equitable access. Coupling vaccination with cervical cancer screening programs establishes a comprehensive prevention framework, maximizing public health benefits. Integrating HPV vaccination into the Universal Immunization Programme ensures equitable access [23]. New quadrivalent vaccines show strong immunogenicity and favourable safety profiles in Indian populations [25, 26]. School-based delivery increases coverage and helps overcome rural access barriers. Adolescents’ misconceptions linking HPV to sexual activity can hinder uptake [31, 32]. CONCLUSION: Research findings clearly indicate that a single-dose HPV vaccine is a practical and affordable choice for India’s healthcare setting. Extending vaccination to boys Sravanthi Malisetty CLS et al Review Article 4333 IJBPAS, September, 2026, 15(9) provides added protection against male cancers while strengthening herd immunity at the population level. In low-resource settings, completing multi-dose vaccination schedules is often difficult, making simplified regimens highly valuable. With proper nationwide implementation, India could achieve the WHO’s 2030 cervical cancer elimination goals and act as a benchmark for other developing countries aiming for equitable, gender-neutral immunization. Key challenges include awareness, infrastructure, and school-based delivery gaps in India [27, 35]. India’s homegrown HPV vaccine, Cervavac, is cheaper and helps the country take a leading role in health collaborations with other developing nations. In the future, it’s important to improve systems that track how well the vaccine works, especially in people who receive only one dose and in boys, to make sure it provides long-lasting protection. JAI DIVYA2 AND RAMA RAO N3 1: Chalapathi Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Affiliated by ANU, Chalapathi, Nagar, Lam, Andhra Pradesh 522034 2: Assistant Professor, Chalapathi Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Affiliated by ANU, Chalapathi, Nagar, Lam, Andhra Pradesh 522034 3: Principal, Professor, Chalapathi Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Affiliated by ANU, Chalapathi, Nagar, Lam, Andhra Pradesh 522034 *Corresponding Author: Chatana Lakshmi Sai Sravanthi Malisetty: E Mail: krhvardhini2005@gmail.com https://doi.org/10.31032/IJBPAS/2026/15.9.10462 ABSTRACT In India, cervical cancer continues to affect many women, though it is largely preventable through HPV vaccines. Recent Indian studies suggest that a single dose may be enough for lasting protection, which is especially useful where access to healthcare is limited. There is rising focus on vaccinating boys, which provides protection against HPV-associated cancers in males while also decreasing community-level infection. The evidence reviewed here points to the potential of these interventions to fast-track India’s efforts in meeting cervical cancer elimination targets. Keywords: Human papillomavirus; Single-dose HPV vaccination; Male HPV vaccination; Cervical cancer prevention; Gender-neutral immunization; Cost-effectiveness; India; Cervavac INTRODUCTION Given the global cervical cancer burden, India bears nearly 20%, with reports around 123,000 of new diagnosis and 77,000 deaths per year [1]. The types 16 and 18 are the Received 29th Sept. 2025; Revised 18th Oct. 2025; Accepted 22nd March 2026; Available online 1st Sept. 2026 Sravanthi Malisetty CLS et al Review Article 4328 IJBPAS, September, 2026, 15(9) high-risk HPV strains which show a persistent infection hold account for nearly 70% of these cases [1, 5]. Protection against HPV16/18 persists for at least 5 years after a single dose [17]. Despite the proven role of HPV vaccination, two- or three dose schedules remain the global standard. Evidence is increasingly showing that a one- dose regimen could achieve adequate and sustained defence against infection [1-3]. At the same time, shifted interest in vaccinating boys enhances its potential to boost herd immunity and reduce the wider impact of HPV associated cancers in both genders. So, while still making cervical cancer elimination as the primary goal, we need to make sure to follow gender neutral vaccination and simple one dose regimen which helps in redefining the strategy on india. One-dose HPV vaccination could prevent a majority of cervical cancers in India, making it highly cost-effective [11]. The review highlights the India’s shifting HPV vaccination policies, focusing on research that validates one-dose protection and the public health benefits of male vaccination. THE CRITICAL ROLE OF HPV VACCINATION IN CANCER PREVENTION: A single dose of HPV vaccine can help cut down cervical cancer incidence and reduce overall costs in India, though gaps in vaccination coverage remain a concern [36, 37]. In South Asia, uptake is low at about 8%, but improving knowledge and awareness can increase acceptance. Even with lower antibody responses, a single dose still provides effective protection compared with multiple doses [38, 39]. HPV vaccines are widely regarded as safe, protective, and economically beneficial. Offering a single dose to 10-year-old girls in India proves more cost-effective than giving two doses [40, 41]. The recently tested quadrivalent vaccine has shown excellent safety and immune response in both girls and boys aged 9–14, and both one- and two-dose regimens work well if given before exposure [42, 43]. India’s indigenous vaccine highlights progress, yet barriers like limited awareness and access continue. Long-term results reveal about 95% protection up to 10 years, supporting inclusion in the UIP [44, 45]. Widespread adolescent vaccination could prevent up to 90% of cervical cancer cases. Persistent hurdles include limited epidemiological clarity, mixed parental attitudes, and gaps in monitoring. Vaccine efficacy remains highest when given between ages 9 and 14 [46-48]. A single dose has shown strong protection against HPV-16 in Indian girls, yet overall uptake in South Asia is still poor, with awareness continuing to be the strongest predictor of acceptance [49, 50]. EVIDENCE FOR ONE DOSE HPV VACCINATON IN INDIA: Sravanthi Malisetty CLS et al Review Article 4329 IJBPAS, September, 2026, 15(9) Indian research, in collaboration with IARC, provides robust data validating the effectiveness of single-dose HPV vaccination. Basu et al. [1, 18] reported long-term outcomes showing that protection against HPV-16/18 infection persisted for at least a decade, with efficacy from a single dose approximating that of multidose regimens. Longitudinal immunogenicity analysis also confirmed durable antibody levels after one dose [2], and further observational work showed reduced new HPV infections [5]. Economic and modeling analyses further emphasize the potential of this approach, showing that single-dose programs could be both impactful in reducing cervical cancer and financially practical for India [3, 4, 16]. Studies indicate that a one-dose HPV vaccination plan offers nearly 50% savings compared to multi-dose regimens while still delivering strong protection levels. For resource-constrained settings such as India, this cost-effectiveness could make large-scale vaccination programs more feasible. Yet, it remains important to track recipients long-term to confirm durability and address potential risks of waning immunity. Single-dose schedules provide comparable long-term protection as two- or three-dose regimens [12, 15, 19, 20]. Single-dose vaccination effectively reduces cervical precancerous lesions (CIN2+) [30]. title: Factors Affecting Cervical Cancer Screening in Primary Care Physician Practices in Ukraine
abstract: Abstract Purpose Cervical cancer remains a major cause of cancer-related deaths among women in Ukraine. Screening efforts are limited by systemic challenges and the ongoing conflict. This study assessed cervical cancer screening practices, barriers, and facilitators among primary care physicians in Ukraine. Methods We conducted a national cross-sectional survey of internal medicine and family medicine physicians in April-May 2023. The survey gathered data on clinical practices, access to screening tools, use of screening tests, and perceived barriers. Results were analyzed using descriptive statistics and adjusted population estimates. Results Among 292 respondents, most primary care physicians referred patients to gynecologists for cervical cancer screening rather than performing screening themselves. Direct use of screening tests was low: 19.5% used Papanicolaou (Pap) tests, 20.2% used Pap and human papillomavirus (HPV) co-testing, 5.8% used HPV testing, and 4.1% offered self-collection HPV tests. Only 13% of practices had Pap tests available. Key barriers included limited training on the benefits of screening and counseling patients (43.8%), lack of equipment or supplies (34.2%), and absence of reimbursement for procedures (27.7%). Patient-related barriers included low awareness of screening (41.8%), financial constraints (36.0%), and fear of treatment (35.3%). Physicians familiar with national guidelines and with access to screening tools were more likely to implement screening practices. Conclusion Gaps in training, resources, and systemic support constrain cervical cancer screening in Ukraine’s primary care settings. Improving physician education, access to diagnostic tools, and adherence to national guidelines may help to enhance screening uptake and reduce cervical cancer burden.

Context Summary Key Objective: What factors influence cervical cancer screening practices among primary care physicians (PCPs) in Ukraine, and what barriers and facilitators do they face? Knowledge Generated: Among 292 surveyed Ukrainian PCPs, 92.1% rely on referrals to gynecologists rather than performing screening themselves, while fewer than 21% use Pap or HPV/Pap co-testing directly. Familiarity with Ministry of Health guidelines is associated with higher screening rates (e.g., Pap test use: 21.7% vs. 11.5% among physicians unaware of the guidelines). Key barriers include insufficient training, limited availability of screening equipment, and patient-level factors such as low awareness of screening and fear of treatment. Relevance: Cervical cancer remains a major public health burden in Ukraine, with over 3,000 new cases annually. The findings identify actionable gaps - particularly in PCP training, resource availability, and guideline dissemination - that, if addressed, could support progress toward WHO cervical cancer elimination targets. INTRODUCTION Page 3/22 Cervical cancer ranks as the fourth most common cancer affecting women globally 1. In 2022, there were an estimated 662,301 new cases and 348,874 deaths from cervical cancer worldwide, with the highest incidence and mortality rates (>90%) found in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs)2. The age-standardized incidence rate for cervical cancer in 2022 was 14.1, while the mortality rate was 7.1 per 100,000 people2 globally. In Ukraine, an estimated 3,004 new cases of cervical cancer are diagnosed annually (14.4 per 100,000 women)3,4, and 1,106 women die of cervical cancer, representing 5.5% of the 54,625 new cancer cases and 5.9% of all cancer-related deaths. Cervical cancer ranks fifth in incidence and ninth in mortality 5. Cervical cancer screening has strong evidence supporting prevention and early diagnosis to reduce mortality6,7. Ukraine lacked population-based Comprehensive Cancer Screening programs or guidelines before 2017 8. In 2017, the healthcare system in Ukraine underwent significant reforms, focusing on primary care, disease screening, and prevention8. This led to the establishment of the National Health Service of Ukraine (NHSU). The Ministry of Health (MOH) issued a public guideline on June 18, 2024, addressing key aspects of an effective cervical cancer screening program and introducing a national standard for cervical cancer screening. Updated guidelines for implementing screening were published on August 5, 2024. These policies highlight the importance of evidence-based practices, such as routine Papanicolaou (Pap) testing, HPV/Pap co-testing, treatment of women screened positive, and HPV vaccination, in reducing the disease burden. These reforms aim to create standardized protocols for early detection, prevention, and treatment, enhancing women’s health in Ukraine9. Almost all (99%) cases of cervical cancer are caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, making HPV vaccination a critical primary prevention strategy10. In Ukraine, the HPV vaccination program has faced several challenges, resulting in low vaccination coverage and limited access for the population 11. The HPV vaccine is not included in the national immunization program, and patients must pay for it out of pocket 12,13. This financial barrier has reduced vaccine uptake. Furthermore, the HPV vaccination program in Ukraine has primarily focused on teenage females, as cervical cancer mainly affects the female population 14. The Cervical Cancer Elimination Initiative has established national targets, known as the 90-70-90 targets, for countries to eliminate cervical cancer by 2030. These targets require that 90% of girls receive the complete HPV vaccine before turning 15 years old, 70% of women undergo high-performance screenings at ages 35 and 45, and 90% of women with precancerous lesions or invasive cancer receive prompt treatment 15. The Ukrainian healthcare system faces numerous challenges in primary care due to limited resources and outdated infrastructure, making it difficult to provide high-quality care 16,17. Previous research has identified several barriers that hinder the effective implementation of cervical cancer screening and HPV vaccination in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). These barriers include limited access to healthcare services, such as screening facilities equipped for pelvic exams, Pap tests, and a shortage of trained healthcare providers to treat pre- cancer/cancer 18. Other factors include insufficient awareness and knowledge about cervical cancer and the benefits of screening and vaccination, cultural beliefs and stigmas surrounding reproductive health issues, and cost constraints19. Our study aimed to identify the factors that influence cervical cancer screening and the perceived barriers and facilitators that primary care physicians (PCPs) in Ukraine face. The results of our research may be beneficial for improving cervical cancer screening in Ukraine and creating national screening programs. METHODS Survey Design and Distribution, Data Collection Tool Design, and Allocation We designed a survey for Ukrainian primary care providers to evaluate factors associated with cervical cancer screening. The survey questions were created to capture the experiences, attitudes, and practices related to cervical cancer screening and were adapted from the National Cancer Institute’s Survey of Colorectal Screening Practices for primary care physicians Page 4/22 (PCPs) 20,21. The questionnaire was modified to fit the Ukrainian healthcare context. Formal survey validation was beyond the scope and primary aim of this study; however, the survey was adapted from a previously used instrument through discussions with oncology specialists and primary care physicians in Ukraine. Additionally, the survey examined barriers to cancer screening and early diagnosis based on constructs from the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Science (CFIR), the Barriers to Effective Screening Tool, and factors identified in other studies that influence cancer screening and early diagnosis 22–28. The questions addressed the following topics: 1) characteristics of clinical practice; 2) beliefs, knowledge, experience, and practices related to cancer screening; 3) frequency of use of specific cervical cancer screening methods; 4) potential barriers to and facilitators of cervical cancer screening in Ukraine; 5) availability of the HPV vaccine. All participants were asked to define cervical cancer screening through a multiple-choice question that included a “correct” definition of “screening” among the answer options to evaluate their initial knowledge and understanding of screening terminology (select Refer to the Survey Instrument in Supplement 1 for more details). Since respondents could choose multiple options, the totals will not add up to 100% for some of the questions Survey questions were translated into Ukrainian and refined with the assistance of a team of Ukrainian physicians, including a family medicine physician, a surgical oncologist, medical oncologists, and gynecologists. The final electronic survey was distributed to a convenience sample of primary care physicians (PCPs) in Ukraine through the Facebook page of the Academy of Family Medicine of Ukraine, the Global Medical Knowledge Alliance, and a physician- only Facebook group that included over 35,000 members. No financial incentives were offered for participation. The survey was conducted in April and May 2023, and the National Cancer Institute Institutional Review Board in Kyiv, Ukraine, approved the study. In accordance with the journal’s guidelines, we will provide our data for independent analysis by a selected team by the Editorial Team for the purposes of additional data analysis or for the reproducibility of this study in other centers if such is requested. Ethics considerations The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Ukrainian National Cancer Institute. Written informed consent was not required, given the low-risk nature of the study. Participants were provided with information sheets about the study, including the plan to publish the results in aggregate form prior to taking the online survey. Participation was voluntary, and the confidentiality of all respondents was strictly maintained throughout the research process. Data analysis and data interpretation To enable population-level inferences, we utilized publicly available data from the national primary care physician demographics collected by the National Health Service of Ukraine (NHSU). This information is accessible online and includes the marginal distribution of age, gender, specialty, and geographical practice location of primary care physicians in Ukraine. Notably, at the time of the analysis, there were 20,820 primary care physicians (PCPs) in Ukraine, of whom 82,20% were female and 17,80% were male. Out of the 409 collected surveys, 117 were excluded because they lacked demographic data. After excluding physicians from other specialties, only primary care physicians (PCPs) were considered, resulting in a total of 292 out of 409 surveys included in our analysis. In addition to reporting the summary responses from the sample, we also assumed that the conditional distribution for each question response could be appropriately modeled using a binary logistic model if the response had two levels, or a Page 5/22 multinomial logistic model if it had more. We utilized the fitted models to estimate the expected population-level responses by standardizing the results according to the known population marginal distributions of the covariates. To estimate associations between the use of cervical cancer screening tests and responses to survey questions, we fit logistic models for screening test usage, conditional on physician age, gender, specialty, geographical region, and the response to the relevant survey question. Using the fitted model, we then estimated the expected probability of using each cervical cancer screening test based on each level of response to the survey question by directly standardizing to the known population marginal distributions of the covariates. We employed this approach to compute associations between the use of screening tests - specifically, the Pap test and the Pap/HPV co-testing - and the reported use of various educational materials, availability of cervical cancer screening tests, and beliefs about the effectiveness of cervical cancer screening, adjusted for physician age, gender, specialty, and geographical region. Confidence intervals (CIs) were constructed by taking percentiles of the sampling distribution, estimated by bootstrapping with 1000 iterations. We performed statistical analysis using R version 4.2.2. RESULTS Participant demographics and clinical practice characteristics compared to primary care physicians (PCPs) overall in Ukraine Out of the 409 surveys collected, 292 were included in the analysis, comprising 250 (85.6%) family medicine physicians and 42 (14.4%) internal medicine physicians. The majority of respondents were women (92.5%, 270), while men represented 7.5% (22). The age distribution revealed that the largest group of primary care physicians (PCPs) was aged 31–40 years (42.1%), followed by those aged 20–30 years (27.7%) and 41–50 years (21.6%) (Table 1). Survey respondents represented 24 of 25 administrative districts of Ukraine, with the exception of Russian-occupied Crimea. The highest representation came from the western regions, accounting for 44.2% of respondents. (Fig. 1). At the time of data analysis, based on data from the National Health Service of Ukraine (NHSU), there were 20,820 primary care physicians (PCPs) in Ukraine, including 16,994 Family medicine doctors and 3,826 Internal medicine doctors, of whom 82,20% were female and 17,80% were male. The data from the National Health Service of Ukraine (NHSU) also excluded physicians from Russian-occupied Crimea 29. The demographics of the surveyed primary care physicians (PCPs) closely align with national trends. In the dataset from the National Health Service of Ukraine (NHSU), 82% of primary care physicians (PCPs) specialize in family medicine, compared to 85.6% in our study. Cervical Cancer Screening Modalities and Perceptions of Effectiveness A significant percentage of surveyed primary care physicians (PCPs) (92.1%) reported referring patients to gynecologists for cervical cancer screening. However, fewer primary care physicians (PCPs) reported directly using specific screening tests: 20.2% utilized the HPV/Pap co-testing, 19.5% conducted Pap tests, 5.8% performed HPV tests, and only 4.1% provided self- collection HPV tests. A small percentage of primary care physicians (PCPs) (4.5%) did not use any screening modality. In terms of resource availability, 45.9% of primary care physicians (PCPs) reported having access to gynecologists at their clinics. However, access to specific screening tools was limited: 13.0% reported the availability of Pap tests, 13.4% had access to HPV/Pap co-testing, 5.1% could offer self-collection HPV tests, and 4.5% had HPV tests available. Page 6/22 Primary care physicians’ (PCPs’) perceptions of the effectiveness of screening modalities varied. Most respondents, 84.9%, believed the HPV/Pap co-testing was very effective in reducing cervical cancer mortality. In comparison, 54.8% believed in the effectiveness of Pap tests, 45.2% supported HPV tests, and only 16.1% viewed self-HPV testing as very effective (Table 2). Read Full License Page 1/22 Additional Declarations: No competing interests reported. Page 2/22 Abstract Purpose Cervical cancer remains a major cause of cancer-related deaths among women in Ukraine. Screening efforts are limited by systemic challenges and the ongoing conflict. This study assessed cervical cancer screening practices, barriers, and facilitators among primary care physicians in Ukraine. Methods We conducted a national cross-sectional survey of internal medicine and family medicine physicians in April-May 2023. The survey gathered data on clinical practices, access to screening tools, use of screening tests, and perceived barriers. Results were analyzed using descriptive statistics and adjusted population estimates. Results Among 292 respondents, most primary care physicians referred patients to gynecologists for cervical cancer screening rather than performing screening themselves. Direct use of screening tests was low: 19.5% used Papanicolaou (Pap) tests, 20.2% used Pap and human papillomavirus (HPV) co-testing, 5.8% used HPV testing, and 4.1% offered self-collection HPV tests. Only 13% of practices had Pap tests available. Key barriers included limited training on the benefits of screening and counseling patients (43.8%), lack of equipment or supplies (34.2%), and absence of reimbursement for procedures (27.7%). Patient-related barriers included low awareness of screening (41.8%), financial constraints (36.0%), and fear of treatment (35.3%). Physicians familiar with national guidelines and with access to screening tools were more likely to implement screening practices. Conclusion Gaps in training, resources, and systemic support constrain cervical cancer screening in Ukraine’s primary care settings. Improving physician education, access to diagnostic tools, and adherence to national guidelines may help to enhance screening uptake and reduce cervical cancer burden. Context Summary Key Objective: What factors influence cervical cancer screening practices among primary care physicians (PCPs) in Ukraine, and what barriers and facilitators do they face? Knowledge Generated: Among 292 surveyed Ukrainian PCPs, 92.1% rely on referrals to gynecologists rather than performing screening themselves, while fewer than 21% use Pap or HPV/Pap co-testing directly. Familiarity with Ministry of Health guidelines is associated with higher screening rates (e.g., Pap test use: 21.7% vs. 11.5% among physicians unaware of the guidelines). Key barriers include insufficient training, limited availability of screening equipment, and patient-level factors such as low awareness of screening and fear of treatment. Relevance: Cervical cancer remains a major public health burden in Ukraine, with over 3,000 new cases annually. The findings identify actionable gaps - particularly in PCP training, resource availability, and guideline dissemination - that, if addressed, could support progress toward WHO cervical cancer elimination targets. INTRODUCTION Page 3/22 Cervical cancer ranks as the fourth most common cancer affecting women globally 1. In 2022, there were an estimated 662,301 new cases and 348,874 deaths from cervical cancer worldwide, with the highest incidence and mortality rates (>90%) found in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs)2. The age-standardized incidence rate for cervical cancer in 2022 was 14.1, while the mortality rate was 7.1 per 100,000 people2 globally. In Ukraine, an estimated 3,004 new cases of cervical cancer are diagnosed annually (14.4 per 100,000 women)3,4, and 1,106 women die of cervical cancer, representing 5.5% of the 54,625 new cancer cases and 5.9% of all cancer-related deaths. Cervical cancer ranks fifth in incidence and ninth in mortality 5. Cervical cancer screening has strong evidence supporting prevention and early diagnosis to reduce mortality6,7. Ukraine lacked population-based Comprehensive Cancer Screening programs or guidelines before 2017 8. In 2017, the healthcare system in Ukraine underwent significant reforms, focusing on primary care, disease screening, and prevention8. This led to the establishment of the National Health Service of Ukraine (NHSU). The Ministry of Health (MOH) issued a public guideline on June 18, 2024, addressing key aspects of an effective cervical cancer screening program and introducing a national standard for cervical cancer screening. Updated guidelines for implementing screening were published on August 5, 2024. These policies highlight the importance of evidence-based practices, such as routine Papanicolaou (Pap) testing, HPV/Pap co-testing, treatment of women screened positive, and HPV vaccination, in reducing the disease burden. These reforms aim to create standardized protocols for early detection, prevention, and treatment, enhancing women’s health in Ukraine9. Almost all (99%) cases of cervical cancer are caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, making HPV vaccination a critical primary prevention strategy10. In Ukraine, the HPV vaccination program has faced several challenges, resulting in low vaccination coverage and limited access for the population 11. The HPV vaccine is not included in the national immunization program, and patients must pay for it out of pocket 12,13. This financial barrier has reduced vaccine uptake. Furthermore, the HPV vaccination program in Ukraine has primarily focused on teenage females, as cervical cancer mainly affects the female population 14. The Cervical Cancer Elimination Initiative has established national targets, known as the 90-70-90 targets, for countries to eliminate cervical cancer by 2030. These targets require that 90% of girls receive the complete HPV vaccine before turning 15 years old, 70% of women undergo high-performance screenings at ages 35 and 45, and 90% of women with precancerous lesions or invasive cancer receive prompt treatment 15. The Ukrainian healthcare system faces numerous challenges in primary care due to limited resources and outdated infrastructure, making it difficult to provide high-quality care 16,17. Previous research has identified several barriers that hinder the effective implementation of cervical cancer screening and HPV vaccination in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). These barriers include limited access to healthcare services, such as screening facilities equipped for pelvic exams, Pap tests, and a shortage of trained healthcare providers to treat pre- cancer/cancer 18. Other factors include insufficient awareness and knowledge about cervical cancer and the benefits of screening and vaccination, cultural beliefs and stigmas surrounding reproductive health issues, and cost constraints19. Our study aimed to identify the factors that influence cervical cancer screening and the perceived barriers and facilitators that primary care physicians (PCPs) in Ukraine face. full_text: Abstract Background Vulvar cancer is a rare gynecological malignancy accounting for approximately 5% of female genital tract cancers. Women living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are at increased risk because impaired cellular immunity predisposes them to persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and accelerated progression to dysplasia and malignancy. Compared to the general population, vulvar carcinoma in women living with HIV presents at a younger age and is often multifocal. Case Report We report a rare case of a 41-year-old woman living with HIV diagnosed with moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma arising from the superior mons pubis without involvement of the labia or clitoris. The unusual anatomical location and unifocal presentation posed significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Following multidisciplinary consultation, the patient underwent staged surgical management with adjuvant radiotherapy. Radical excision with simultaneous bilateral inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy was considered impractical because of anatomical limitations and inadequate tissue for wound closure while maintaining surgical margins. Although musculocutaneous flap reconstruction was planned, intraoperative difficulty in identifying the vascular pedicle of the tensor fascia lata flap necessitated temporary wound management using Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) dressing. Split-thickness skin grafting was later performed after reduction in wound size, followed by bilateral inguinofemoral lymph node dissection. Discussion To our knowledge, vulvar carcinoma presenting as a solitary lesion over the superior mons pubis has not previously been reported. Initial suspicion of a primary cutaneous malignancy was excluded by p16-positive immunohistochemistry. Conclusion This case highlights the importance of individualized multidisciplinary management and maintaining high clinical suspicion for atypical vulvar lesions in immunocompromised women. title: Case report: Penile collision tumor comprising HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma and malignant melanoma
abstract: Collision tumors with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and malignant melanoma components are extremely rare. We report a case of a penile collision tumor with a component of HPV-associated SCC and malignant melanoma in a 61 year-old man. The patient underwent a partial penectomy and bilateral inguinal sentinel lymph node surgery. Microscopy showed a biphasic tumor with a component of SCC with warty-basaloid morphology, positive for HPV16 and 43, and a malignant melanoma associated with a BRAF mutation. This case posed diagnostic and therapeutic challenges due to the absence of a precise TNM classification and documented treatment guidelines for this tumor type.
